result: The manuscript documents the timeline of COVID-19 in Canada during the first and second waves, including the first case detection on 25 January 2020, implementation of travel restrictions in March 2020, and peak case counts in May 2020 (first wave) and January 2021 (second wave).
evaluation: Claims C1-C9, C13, and C23 provide a consistent chronological account of COVID-19 events in Canada with specific dates and case counts. These claims are supported by citations to external sources (Press, 2021) and reference to data visualizations (Figure 1C), providing converging evidence for the timeline.

result: The manuscript characterizes the geographic and lineage distribution of early COVID-19 cases in Canada, with A.1 and B.4 lineages predominant in British Columbia, B.1* and B.1.1* lineages in Ontario and Quebec, and B.1.279 in Alberta during March-June 2020.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 describe the spatial and lineage distribution of early cases with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The claims are internally consistent and supported by phylogenetic data presented in the manuscript.

result: The manuscript documents the emergence and detection of variants of concern (VOCs) and variants of interest (VOIs) in Canada, with B.1.1.7 (Alpha) first detected on 8 November 2020, followed by multiple other variants through early 2021, which drove the second and third waves.
evaluation: Claims C14-C28 provide a comprehensive timeline of VOC/VOI detection with specific dates attributed to GISAID data. The claims are internally consistent and describe the epidemiological impact of these variants on subsequent waves, supported by the phylogenetic analysis presented.

result: The phylogenetic analysis identified 2263 (95% CI: 2159-2366) total SARS-CoV-2 introductions into Canada by the end of February 2021, comprising 680 (658-703) Canadian sublineages and 1582 (1501-1663) singletons.
evaluation: Claims C29-C31 present the primary quantitative findings from the phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals. These estimates are derived from the maximum likelihood phylogenetic approach described in the methods and are consistent across multiple bootstrap replicates, providing robust support.

result: The manuscript identifies the geographic origins of SARS-CoV-2 sublineages in Canada, with 49% (46-52%) of first wave sublineages originating from the USA (primarily introduced into Quebec and Ontario), while the second wave showed continued USA predominance (43%) alongside increased contributions from India (16%) and the UK (7%).
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 describe the geographic origins of viral introductions with confidence intervals. These findings are supported by the phylogeographic analysis (Figure 3) and are consistent with the subsampling sensitivity analysis, demonstrating robustness across different analytical strategies.

result: The manuscript demonstrates that travel restrictions implemented on 21 March 2020 drastically reduced SARS-CoV-2 importations, with the importation rate declining from 58.5 (50.4-66.5) sublineages per week to 10.3-fold (8.3-15.0) lower within 4 weeks, though with variable effectiveness across provinces.
evaluation: Claims C37, C86-C99 provide detailed quantitative evidence for the impact of travel restrictions on viral importations. The temporal association between policy implementation and importation rate changes is supported by phylogenetic dating (Figure 4) and is robust across multiple subsampling strategies (Figure 6—figure supplement 5). The provincial variation in effectiveness is documented with confidence intervals.

result: By the end of February 2021, an estimated 30 (19-41) B.1.1.7 sublineages had been imported into Canada, which increasingly displaced previously circulating sublineages by the end of the second wave.
evaluation: Claims C38, C39, and C68 describe the importation and competitive dynamics of B.1.1.7 (Alpha variant). The quantitative estimates are supported by phylogenetic analysis with confidence intervals, and the displacement of earlier lineages is consistent with the known increased transmissibility of this variant.

result: The phylogenetic analysis estimated the time to most recent common ancestor (TMRCA) as 22 December 2019 (24 November-23 December) and molecular clock rates of 2.86 × 10⁻⁴ (relaxed clock, LSD2) and 7.15 × 10⁻⁴ (strict clock, TempEst) substitutions/site/year.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 present phylogenetic parameter estimates with confidence intervals and appropriate citations to prior work. The TMRCA estimate is consistent with other published estimates, and the difference between relaxed and strict clock rates is appropriately attributed to differing model assumptions.

result: The manuscript reports that 75.1% of sublineages were supported by high likelihoods (>0.9) in both introduction and parental nodes across all bootstraps.
evaluation: Claim C43 describes the statistical support for phylogenetic inferences with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3. This provides important validation of the reliability of the ancestral state reconstruction used to identify viral introductions.

result: The manuscript demonstrates extreme overdispersion in sublineage sizes, with 14 sublineages (2.3% of total) having ≥500 descendants accounting for 59.1% of all Canadian sublineage descendants, and 46 sublineages with >100 descendants accounting for 77% (74-81%) of Canadian sequences.
evaluation: Claims C44-C45 and C82-C85 describe the highly skewed distribution of sublineage sizes with specific quantitative estimates and confidence intervals. This finding is supported by Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2, demonstrating that a small number of introductions drove the majority of cases.

result: During the first wave (1 January to 31 July 2020), there were 384 (368-400) introductions resulting in domestic transmission, with detailed breakdown by Pango lineage including 169 (155-182) B.1, 53 (50-56) B.1.1, 23 (20-25) A.1, and other sublineages.
evaluation: Claims C46-C52 provide detailed quantitative characterization of first wave introductions by lineage with confidence intervals. These estimates are derived from the phylogenetic analysis and are supported by Figure 3A, providing comprehensive documentation of viral diversity during the first wave.

result: The manuscript identifies the geographic origins of first wave Canadian sublineages, with the USA as the predominant source (49%, 46-52%), followed by Russia (12%, 11-13%), Italy (6%, 5-9%), India (6%, 5-7%), Spain (5%, 4-5%), and the UK (4%, 4-5%).
evaluation: Claims C53-C58 provide detailed geographic attribution of first wave sublineages with confidence intervals. These findings are supported by the phylogeographic analysis and are consistent with global COVID-19 epidemiology during this period.

result: First wave sublineages were primarily imported into Quebec (39%, 38-40%) and Ontario (36%, 35-38%), followed by British Columbia (12%, 11-13%), with smaller contributions to other provinces.
evaluation: Claims C59-C65 describe the provincial distribution of first wave importations with confidence intervals. These findings are supported by the phylogeographic analysis and are consistent with population sizes and international connectivity of these provinces.

result: The second wave (1 August 2020 to 28 February 2021) included 296 (280-313) newly introduced sublineages, primarily B.1.2 (55, 54-56), B.1.1.7 (30, 19-40), B.1.36 (24, 22-25), B.1 (14, 12-15), and B.1.1.519 (8, 8-9) lineages.
evaluation: Claims C66-C71 provide detailed quantitative characterization of second wave introductions by lineage with confidence intervals. These estimates are derived from the phylogenetic analysis and are supported by Figure 3B, documenting the shift in viral diversity including emergence of VOCs.

result: The origins of second wave sublineages remained predominantly from the USA (43%, 40-45%), with increased relative contributions from India (16%, 15-17%), the UK (7%, 5-9%), Asia (6%, 5-6%), Europe (4%, 4-5%), and Africa (3%, 3-4%).
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 describe the geographic origins of second wave sublineages with confidence intervals. The diversification of source countries compared to the first wave is well-documented and reflects changing global epidemiology and travel patterns.

result: During the second wave, there were relatively more sublineages introduced to Ontario (45%, 44-47%), British Columbia (23%, 22-24%), and Alberta (11%, 10-11%), and fewer to Quebec (16%, 16-17%) compared to the first wave.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 describe the shift in provincial distribution of importations between waves with confidence intervals. This finding is supported by the phylogeographic analysis and may reflect changes in travel patterns, testing capacity, or public health measures across provinces.

result: The manuscript concludes that wild-type sublineages introduced in summer 2020 when prevalence and immunity were low contributed the highest proportion of COVID-19 cases in the second wave.
evaluation: Claim C100 is supported by the temporal analysis of sublineage contributions shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4. The finding that summer introductions drove second wave cases despite low importation rates demonstrates the importance of sustained interventions.

result: The manuscript documents that overall international arrivals into Canada declined 77.8% from 96.8M in 2019 to 19.7M in 2020, but truck drivers and crew members declined only 24.8%, accounting for 49% of arrivals after April 2020, with 14.6M Canadian and 5.1M non-resident arrivals in 2020.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 provide contextual data on travel patterns with citation to Canada Statistics. These data help interpret the phylogenetic findings regarding continued importations despite travel restrictions, particularly the role of essential workers.

result: The manuscript notes that mandatory 3-day hotel quarantine for international arrivals by air was not implemented until 22 February 2021.
evaluation: Claim C105 is a factual statement about policy timing with citation to Government of Canada sources. This contextualizes the continued importations observed during the study period.

result: The manuscript reports that 1,999,711 SARS-CoV-2 sequences were downloaded from GISAID on 17 June 2021, of which 63,645 were sampled in Canada, with 495,159 sequences representing 108,301,802 diagnoses globally by 15 June 2021.
evaluation: Claims C106, C113-C114 describe the data sources with appropriate citations to GISAID. These claims document the scale of genomic surveillance and provide context for the subsampling strategies employed.

result: The manuscript states that phylogenetic analyses depend on timely sequence sharing and that VOCs have demonstrated increased transmissibility, potential increased clinical severity, and ability to circumvent host immune responses.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108 are general knowledge statements about phylogenetic methods and VOC characteristics, appropriately supported by citations to relevant literature. These provide important context for the study's rationale.

result: The manuscript cites prior phylogenetic studies estimating 1179 introductions in the UK, a single introduction driving Louisiana's first wave, 277 introductions in New Zealand (19% with multiple descendants), and at least 500 introductions into Quebec by June 2020.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 accurately cite prior phylogenetic studies with appropriate references. These provide important comparative context for interpreting the Canadian findings, though the accuracy of these prior estimates depends on the cited sources.

result: Canadian viral genomes represented 345 unique Pango lineages dispersed throughout the global phylogeny, with 34,169 (31,337-37,001) sampled descendants identified, including 25,270 (25,071-26,369) in Canada and 8449 (5915-10,983) global descendants (vastly underestimated by subsampling).
evaluation: Claims C115-C119 describe the phylogenetic diversity and descendant distribution with confidence intervals. The acknowledgment that global descendants were underestimated due to subsampling (C119) demonstrates appropriate recognition of methodological limitations.

result: The manuscript notes that no sequences were available from Yukon, Northwest Territories, Nunavut, or Prince Edward Island, which cumulatively had 603 COVID-19 cases (0.07% of Canada cases) prior to 1 March 2021.
evaluation: Claims C120-C121 document data availability limitations. The small case burden in these territories (0.07%) suggests minimal impact on overall findings, though this represents a geographic gap in the analysis.

result: Prior to travel restrictions, provinces had a mean of 26% of transmission events with international origins (ranging from 17% in Saskatchewan to 33% in British Columbia), while in April 2020, Ontario and Quebec retained relatively high mean numbers of international transmission events at 115 (105-125) and 95 (82-109) respectively.
evaluation: Claims C122-C123 describe the proportion and absolute numbers of international transmission sources with confidence intervals, supported by Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The persistence of international transmission in Ontario and Quebec after restrictions is an important finding.

result: During the first wave, Ontario and Quebec were the greatest sampled sources of interprovincial transmission, while in the second wave Ontario remained the greatest source followed by nearly equal contributions from British Columbia, Alberta, and Quebec.
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 describe interprovincial transmission patterns supported by Figure 5B. These findings document the role of domestic transmission in sustaining the epidemic and the shift in transmission dynamics between waves.

result: Sublineage size and transmission lifespan were significantly reduced over time among both active and extinct sublineages (both p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C126-C127 report statistically significant temporal trends with p-values and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The findings suggest improving outbreak control over time, though the emergence of VOCs may have altered these dynamics.

result: Average sublineage detection lag did not change significantly over time (p=0.62), and there was insufficient evidence that detection lag was significantly associated with province of introduction (Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.23).
evaluation: Claims C128-C129 report non-significant statistical findings with appropriate p-values and test specifications. These negative results are important for understanding surveillance capacity and are appropriately reported with references to Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.
